opening.headline: If an API key has been posted to a public repository, what should be done first, and what should be verified?
body: Anyone who knows the key can call the model using our account. Costs and data are simultaneously at risk, and if multiple services share the same key, it becomes difficult to determine where and how it is being used.

In this lesson, we sequentially examine the steps of deactivation, replacement, and log review corresponding to leaked keys. We analyze a single audit log line to identify which fields should be examined, and illustrate with an example how incorrect log analysis can lead to the erroneous conclusion that no damage has occurred.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the thank-you logs and key exposure response procedures
Analysis of query conditions that track the exposure scope in logs is possible.

screens.title: API key has been leaked
screens.lead: At the moment the key is leaked, review the situation the team faces.

paragraphs: We received a notification that a commit containing an API key has been pushed to a public repository. Anyone who knows the key can call our model using our account. The call costs will be billed to our account, and the data contained in the request and response is also exposed to risk.

There is a factor that makes the situation more complicated. When multiple services share the same key, it becomes difficult to determine the source of the leak or which service has been affected. The OWASP Secret Management Guide also notes that it is hard to identify the source of a leak when services share the same secret.

Immediately after receiving a notification, you may feel the urge to act quickly. At this point, deciding what to do first and what to verify later determines the extent of potential damage. The question posed in this lesson is: what should you do first, and what should you verify later?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Will removing the key from a commit resolve the issue? Consider where you might still be able to see the key after it has been removed.

screens.outro: First, let's recall the current state of our team.

screens.title: View: Does the disposal procedure exist when keys are leaked?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Please first think through the question on your own before entering an answer.

items.prompt: Is there a disposal procedure in case of key exposure?
items.answer: Even if a procedure is documented, if it has never been actually implemented, it becomes a first-time experience. When a new procedure is created during an incident, it tends to be discarded later, leading to increased misuse.

items.prompt: Who has the authority to dispose?
items.answer: If permissions are granted to only one person, the system will stop shutting down when that person is not present. Conversely, if everyone has the ability to shut down, the service might be accidentally terminated. It is necessary to predefine who can shut down the system and up to what scope.

items.prompt: How long does it take to deploy a new key?
items.answer: If replacement takes too long, it becomes difficult to decide on disposal. Disposal would stop the service. New keys must be deployed quickly so that disposal can be decided without hesitation.

screens.outro: Now let's look at the response order.

screens.title: Key revocation, replacement, log verification order
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to follow the order corresponding to the leaked keys and to see why each step is in its current position.

visual.alt: Flowchart consisting of three sequential steps: disposal, replacement, and log verification.
labels: 1. Disposal: Immediately invalidate any leaked keys
2. Replacement: Issue new key, deploy only to required services
3. Log Verification: Call Tracing in the Section Prior to Disposal

steps.title: Step 1: Discard the leaked key
steps.body: Immediately invalidate the leaked key. Disposal comes first because misuse could continue even while logs are being reviewed. The OWASP guide also states that if sensitive information is no longer needed or if there is a possibility it has been leaked, it should be securely disposed of and access restricted.

steps.title: Editing code or restarting is not disposal.
steps.body: Removing a key from a commit does not remove it from repository history. Restarting the service does not invalidate stolen credentials. A stolen key remains valid until the key itself is revoked.

steps.title: Step 2: Issue a new key and replace it.
steps.body: Issue a new key and deploy it only to the necessary services. If each service has its own separate key, you only need to replace the keys affected by the issue. However, if keys were shared across services, you would need to update all services using that key, making the replacement process slower.

steps.title: Step 3: Verify the logs from the disposal prior phase.
steps.body: After disposal, we trace what was called using that key. By examining the logs from before disposal, we can determine whether external calls were made and which data and costs were affected. While the verification occurs later, it is not omitted.

steps.title: Reduce reliance on human labor through automation
steps.body: OWASP recommends automating the generation and rotation of secrets as part of a pipeline to minimize human intervention. Manual maintenance increases exposure risks and is prone to human error. When automatic rotation is in place, key replacement following a leak occurs much faster and more securely.

screens.outro: Once decommissioning and replacement are complete, it's now time to review the logs.

screens.title: Read a thank you log line and track exposure scope
screens.lead: The following is an example line from a configured audit log. Check the right-side descriptions to see how each field is used to track exposure scope, and identify symptoms that appear when there is a mismatch.

notes.note: ts is the timestamp of the request. Since it serves as the basis for splitting logs into exposure intervals, clock desynchronization can cause interval filtering to malfunction. OWASP explains that accurate timestamps are essential in audit logs and that systems must be time-synchronized.
key_id indicates which key was used to make the call. If multiple services share the same key, this value alone cannot distinguish who used it, and thus cannot narrow the scope of impact.

The service is the one that was called. If keys are separated by service, then this value directly affects the affected service. If there is another service using the same key, it must also be included within the impacted scope.

model, src_ip, tokens are fields used for comparison against baseline values. The presence of a previously unused model, an unfamiliar IP address, or unusually high token counts indicates external usage conditions. If these fields are empty, there is no reference point for comparison, making judgment impossible.

screens.outro: Now that I've learned how to read logs, I'll fix an example of incorrect log queries.

screens.title: Analysis: Correcting the impacted scope by reading incorrect log queries
screens.lead: The following is the first query record after the incident. When a highlighted section is selected, the instructor explains what went wrong and how to correct it.

data.text: Situation: The key key-7f3a was committed on Monday at 10:00 and was discovered on Wednesday at 15:00, and was immediately revoked. First query: from=Wednesday 15:00, key_id=key-new, Result: 0 items, so it is presumed no damage occurred.. Modified query: from=Monday 10:00, to=Wednesday 15:00, key_id=key-7f3a. Result: Finds rows different from usual values by combining src_ip and model.

marks.note: The start time is the discovery time, not the exposure time. Since the leak period begins at 10 a.m. on Monday, this query completely omits the most critical timeframe.
The target of the lookup is not a leaked key, but a newly issued key. Since the new key was issued after expiration, there can be no impersonation attack.

marks.span: Result: 0 items, so it is presumed no damage occurred.
marks.note: Zero results from a query with incorrect conditions is not evidence of safety. No conclusions can be drawn until the range and key ID are properly addressed.
The tracking period is from the exposure time to the disposal time, and the target is the leaked key ID. A call for the spoofing period will be displayed only if both conditions are met.

marks.span: Finds rows different from usual values by combining src_ip and model
marks.note: Putting the results together, it reveals IPs, models, and call volumes that are typically unused. Such activity indicates a high likelihood of external usage. If another service uses the same key, it should also be included within the affected scope.

screens.outro: Once the impact scope has been verified, it must be ensured that the same issue does not recur.

screens.title: Explanation: Prevent recurrence
screens.lead: When you select an item to expand, you can view methods for avoiding key exposure. Please read the instructor's explanations one by one.

items.title: Injects without embedding in code
items.body: If a key is stored in plain text within source code or configuration files, it will be distributed along with the repository. By storing the key in a secret management system and injecting it at runtime, the key remains protected even if the code is publicly available. OWASP explains that secrets should be centrally managed and standardized.

items.title: Separate keys by service
items.body: If each service is issued its own key, you can immediately identify which services are affected when a key is leaked. Shared keys make it difficult to trace the source and require changing all services simultaneously when a key is replaced.

items.title: Automates regular rotation
items.body: Regularly rotating secrets ensures that compromised credentials remain valid for only a short period. Manual rotation is prone to errors, so it should be automated. Rotation strategies include progressive, rapid, and scheduled approaches.

items.title: Minimizes privileges by reducing key scope
items.body: If access privileges are restricted to only the necessary scope, any leakage will be limited to that scope. OWASP explains that engineers should apply the principle of least privilege to ensure they do not have access to all secrets.

screens.outro: I will now summarize the lecture content.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Review the core of this course once again.

paragraphs: If a key is leaked, disposal and replacement must occur first, followed by log verification. This is because misuse could continue during the verification process. Removing the key from code or restarting the service does not substitute for proper disposal.

The scope is tracked through audit logs. The query conditions are defined by the leaked key ID and the time period from exposure to deactivation. A query returning zero results does not prove no impact. Sharing keys makes source tracing difficult, and secret management, automated rotation, and least privilege principles help reduce recurrence.

In practice, it is advisable to pre-prepare draft versions of the authorization for disposal, the replacement procedure, and the log query conditions. Having a draft query condition reduces the risk of confusing segments and key IDs during an incident, leading to incorrect conclusions. Additionally, recording the timestamps of disposal and replacement enables accurate definition of exposure periods later on.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: If the log query result is zero records, first question whether the segment and key ID match.

glossary.def: A record that withstands tampering, documenting who requested and approved what, along with the associated timestamp.
A measure to immediately invalidate the leaked key.
This is an action to issue a new key and deploy it to the required locations.
This involves tracing the usage history of a key through logs to identify affected calls and systems.

misconceptions.myth: Deleting the key from the code resolves it.
misconceptions.fact: The key must be retired as it is retained in the repository history.

misconceptions.myth: The service becomes safer upon restart.
misconceptions.fact: Stolen credentials remain valid until they are explicitly discarded.

misconceptions.myth: Analysis and disposal of logs can be done later.
misconceptions.fact: Deactivation comes first. Abuse could still occur during the analysis phase.

misconceptions.myth: If the log query result is zero records, there is no damage.
misconceptions.fact: If the time range or key ID conditions are incorrect, there is no meaning to zero results. You must query using the leaked keys from the exposure timestamp until the expiration timestamp.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Keys are retired and replaced first.
Track the impact scope using logs from the pre-removal section.
The query conditions are the leaked key ID and the time period from exposure time to disposal time.
Reduces recurrence through secret management, automatic rotation, and least privilege.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: If it is discovered that the key has been leaked, what actions should be taken within the first 10 minutes, and who is authorized to carry out this procedure?

checks.q: Review the correct sequence of response stages when an API key is leaked
items: Dispose of the leaked key immediately
Issue a new key and deploy it only to the required services.
Logs what was called with this key prior to disposal
checks.explain: The reason deactivation comes first is because misuse could continue even during the verification process. After replacement, track the impact scope through logs.
checks.intro: Let's look at the response stages for key exposure in sequence. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: The order is correct. Dispose first, then log the trace.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. While verifying, please reconsider the issue that continues to be exploited.

checks.q:
Commit on Monday at 10:00, expire on Wednesday at 15:00, key key-7f3a was queried under the following conditions and returned zero results. Why can't this be considered "no impact"?  
from=Wednesday 15:00, key_id=key-new
options: The query reports after discovery, not during exposure, because it shows a new key rather than the leaked key.
Logging does not record calls for obsolete keys.
Zero entries always mean that the key has not been used yet.
Because the query range is too short, the results are automatically hidden.
checks.explain: The tracking period spans from the time the key is exposed to the time it is disposed of, and the target is the leaked key ID. This query does not constitute evidence of zero incidents because both conditions are not aligned.

wrong.1: Audit logs serve as evidence for tracking usage history prior to disposal, and records are retained.
wrong.2: If the condition is wrong, zero records means nothing. The range and key must be corrected.
wrong.3: The result is not being hidden; rather, the query conditions are skipping the target.

checks.intro: Review the query conditions that returned zero records; the results are not logged.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes, correct. Both the interval and the target key are misaligned, so there is no basis for zero records.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Please review the query conditions again. The clues lie in what the start time and key ID refer to.
